With Sela (Snp 3.7 6.1)

And at that time Keṇiya was devoted to Sela. Then Sela, while going for a walk escorted by the three hundred young students, approached Keṇiya’s hermitage. He saw the preparations going on, and said to Keṇiya, “Worthy Keṇiya, is your son or daughter being married? Or are you setting up a grand sacrifice? Or has King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha been invited for tomorrow’s meal?”
With Sela (Snp 3.7 7.1)

“There is no marriage, Worthy Sela, and the king is not coming. Rather, I am setting up a grand sacrifice. The ascetic Gotama has arrived at Āpaṇa, together with a large Saṅgha of 1,250 mendicants. He has this good reputation: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’ He has been invited by me for tomorrow’s meal together with the mendicant Saṅgha.” “Did you say ‘the awakened one’?” “I said ‘the awakened one’.” “Did you say ‘the awakened one’?” “I said ‘the awakened one’.”
With Sela (Snp 3.7 8.1)

Then Sela thought: “It’s hard to even find the word ‘awakened one’ in the world. The thirty-two marks of a great man have been handed down in our hymns. A great man who possesses these has only two possible destinies, no other. If he stays at home he becomes a king, a wheel-turning monarch, a just and principled king. His dominion extends to all four sides, he achieves stability in the country, and he possesses the seven treasures. He has the following seven treasures: the wheel, the elephant, the horse, the jewel, the woman, the householder, and the commander as the seventh treasure. He has over a thousand sons who are valiant and heroic, crushing the armies of his enemies. After conquering this land girt by sea, he reigns by principle, without rod or sword. But if he goes forth from the lay life to homelessness, he becomes a perfected one, a fully awakened Buddha, who has cast off the world’s veil.” He said, “But Keṇiya, where is the Blessed One at present, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha?”
With Sela (Snp 3.7 9.1)

When he said this, Keṇiya pointed with his right arm and said, “There, worthy Sela, at that line of blue forest.” Then Sela, together with his young students, approached the Buddha. He said to his young students, “Come quietly, gentlemen, tread gently. For the Buddhas are intimidating, like a lion living alone. When I’m consulting with the ascetic Gotama, don’t interrupt. Wait until I’ve finished speaking.”
With Sela (Snp 3.7 10.1)

Then Sela went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side, and scrutinized the Buddha’s body for the thirty-two marks of a great man. He saw all of them except two, which he had doubts about: whether the private parts were sheathed in a foreskin, and the largeness of the tongue.
With Sela (Snp 3.7 11.1)

Then it occurred to the Buddha, “Sela sees all the marks except two, which he has doubts about: whether the private parts are sheathed in a foreskin, and the largeness of the tongue.” The Buddha used his psychic power to will that Sela would see his private parts sheathed in a foreskin. And he stuck out his tongue and stroked back and forth on his ear holes and nostrils, and covered his entire forehead with his tongue.
With Sela (Snp 3.7 12.1)

Then Sela thought, “The ascetic Gotama possesses the thirty-two marks completely, lacking none. But I don’t know whether or not he is an awakened one. I have heard that brahmins of the past who were elderly and senior, the tutors of tutors, said, ‘Those who are perfected ones, fully awakened Buddhas reveal themselves when praised.’ Why don’t I extoll him in his presence with fitting verses?” Then Sela extolled the Buddha in his presence with fitting verses:
With Sela (Snp 3.7 13.1)

“O Blessed One, your body’s perfect,
you’re radiant, handsome, lovely to behold;
golden colored,
with teeth so white; you’re strong.
With Sela (Snp 3.7 14.1)

The characteristics
of a handsome man,
the marks of a great man,
are all found on your body.
With Sela (Snp 3.7 15.1)

Your eyes are clear, your face is fair,
you’re formidable, upright, majestic.
In the midst of the Saṅgha of ascetics,
you dazzle like the sun.
With Sela (Snp 3.7 16.1)

You’re a mendicant fine to see,
with skin that shines like lustrous gold.
But with such excellent appearance,
what do you want with the ascetic life?
With Sela (Snp 3.7 17.1)

You’re fit to be a king,
a wheel-turning monarch, chief of charioteers,
victorious in the four quarters,
lord of the Black Plum Tree Land.
With Sela (Snp 3.7 18.1)

Aristocrats, nobles, and kings
ought follow your rule.
Gotama, may you reign
as king of kings, lord of mankind!”
With Sela (Snp 3.7 19.1)

“I am a king, Sela”, said the Buddha,
“the supreme king of the teaching.
By the teaching I roll forth the wheel
which cannot be rolled back.”
With Sela (Snp 3.7 20.1)

“You claim to be awakened,” said Sela the brahmin,
“the supreme king of the teaching.
‘I roll forth the teaching’:
so you say, Gotama.
With Sela (Snp 3.7 21.1)

Then who is your general,
the disciple who follows the Teacher’s way?
Who keeps rolling the wheel
of the teaching you rolled forth?”
With Sela (Snp 3.7 22.1)

“By me the wheel was rolled forth,” said the Buddha,
“the supreme wheel of the teaching.
Sāriputta, taking after the Realized One,
keeps it rolling on.
With Sela (Snp 3.7 23.1)

I have known what should be known,
and developed what should be developed,
and given up what should be given up:
and so, brahmin, I am a Buddha.
With Sela (Snp 3.7 24.1)

Dispel your doubt in me—
make up your mind, brahmin!
The sight of a Buddha
is hard to find again.
With Sela (Snp 3.7 25.1)

I am a Buddha, brahmin,
the supreme surgeon,
one of those whose appearance in the world
is hard to find again.
With Sela (Snp 3.7 26.1)

A manifestation of divinity, unequaled,
crusher of Māra’s army;
having subdued all my opponents,
I rejoice, fearing nothing from any quarter.”
With Sela (Snp 3.7 27.1)

“Pay heed, good fellows, to what
is spoken by the Clear-eyed One.
The surgeon, the great hero,
roars like a lion in the jungle.
With Sela (Snp 3.7 28.1)

A manifestation of divinity, unequaled,
crusher of Māra’s army;
who would not be inspired by him,
even one born in a dark class?
With Sela (Snp 3.7 29.1)

Those who wish may follow me;
those who don’t may go.
Right here, I’ll go forth in his presence,
the one of such outstanding wisdom.”
With Sela (Snp 3.7 30.1)

“Sir, if you endorse
the teaching of the Buddha,
we’ll also go forth in his presence,
the one of such outstanding wisdom.”
With Sela (Snp 3.7 31.1)

“These three hundred brahmins
with cupped palms held up, ask:
‘May we lead the spiritual life
in your presence, Blessed One?’”
With Sela (Snp 3.7 32.1)

“The spiritual life is well explained,” said the Buddha,
“apparent in the present life, immediately effective.
Here the going forth isn’t in vain
for one who trains with diligence.”
With Sela (Snp 3.7 33.1)

And the brahmin Sela together with his assembly received the going forth, the ordination in the Buddha’s presence. And when the night had passed Keṇiya had delicious fresh and cooked foods prepared in his own hermitage. Then he had the Buddha informed of the time, saying, “It’s time, worthy Gotama, the meal is ready.” Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to Keṇiya’s hermitage, where he sat down on the seat spread out together with the Saṅgha of mendicants.
With Sela (Snp 3.7 34.1)

Then Keṇiya served and satisfied the mendicant Saṅgha headed by the Buddha with his own hands with delicious fresh and cooked foods. When the Buddha had eaten and washed his hand and bowl, Keṇiya took a low seat and sat to one side. The Buddha expressed his appreciation with these verses:
With Sela (Snp 3.7 35.1)
With Sela (Snp 3.7 36.1)
With Sela (Snp 3.7 37.1)

When the Buddha had expressed his appreciation to Keṇiya the matted-hair ascetic with these verses, he rose from his seat and left. Then Venerable Sela and his assembly, living alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute, soon realized the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. They lived having achieved with their own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness. And Venerable Sela together with his assembly became perfected.
With Sela (Snp 3.7 38.1)
Then Sela with his assembly went to the Buddha. He arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his joined palms toward the Buddha, and said:
With Sela (Snp 3.7 39.1)

“This is the eighth day since
we went for refuge, O Clear-eyed One.
In these seven days, Blessed One,
we’ve become tamed in your teaching.
With Sela (Snp 3.7 40.1)

You are the Buddha, you are the Teacher,
you are the sage who has overcome Māra;
you have cut off the underlying tendencies,
you’ve crossed over, and you bring humanity across.
With Sela (Snp 3.7 41.1)

You have transcended attachments,
your defilements are shattered;
you are a lion free of grasping,
with fear and dread given up.
With Sela (Snp 3.7 42.1)

These three hundred mendicants
stand with cupped palms raised.
Stretch out your feet, great hero:
let these giants bow to the Teacher.”
The Dart (Snp 3.8 1.1)

Unforeseen and unknown
is the extent of this mortal life—
hard and short
and bound to pain.
The Dart (Snp 3.8 2.1)

There is no way that
those born will not die.
On reaching old age death follows:
such is the nature of living creatures.
The Dart (Snp 3.8 3.1)

As ripe fruit
are always in danger of falling,
so mortals once born
are always in danger of death.
The Dart (Snp 3.8 4.1)

As clay pots
made by a potter
all end up being broken,
so is the life of mortals.
The Dart (Snp 3.8 5.1)

Young and old,
foolish and wise—
all go under the sway of death;
all are destined to die.
The Dart (Snp 3.8 6.1)

When those overcome by death
leave this world for the next,
a father cannot protect his son,
nor relatives their kin.
The Dart (Snp 3.8 7.1)

See how, while relatives look on,
wailing profusely,
mortals are led away one by one,
like a cow to the slaughter.
The Dart (Snp 3.8 8.1)

And so the world is stricken
by old age and by death.
That is why the attentive do not grieve,
for they understand the way of the world.
The Dart (Snp 3.8 9.1)

For one whose path you do not know—
not whence they came nor where they went—
you lament in vain,
seeing neither end.
The Dart (Snp 3.8 10.1)

If a bewildered person,
lamenting and self-harming,
could extract any good from that,
then those who see clearly would do the same.
The Dart (Snp 3.8 11.1)

For not by weeping and wailing
will you find peace of heart.
It just gives rise to more suffering,
and distresses your body.
The Dart (Snp 3.8 12.1)

Growing thin and pale,
you hurt yourself.
It does nothing to help the dead:
your lamentation is in vain.
The Dart (Snp 3.8 13.1)

Unless a personage gives up grief,
they fall into suffering all the more.
Bewailing those whose time has come,
you fall under the sway of grief.
The Dart (Snp 3.8 14.1)

See, too, other folk departing,
passing on according to their deeds;
fallen under the sway of death,
beings flounder while still here.
The Dart (Snp 3.8 15.1)

For however they imagine it,
it turns out to be something else.
Such is separation:
see the way of the world!
The Dart (Snp 3.8 16.1)

Even if a human lives
a hundred years or more,
they are parted from their family circle,
they leave this life behind.
The Dart (Snp 3.8 17.1)

Therefore, having learned from the Perfected One,
dispel lamentation.
Seeing the dead and departed, think:
“I cannot escape this.”
The Dart (Snp 3.8 18.1)

As one would extinguish
a blazing refuge with water,
so too an attentive one—a wise,
astute, and skilled person—
would swiftly blow away grief that comes up,
like the wind a tuft of cotton.
The Dart (Snp 3.8 19.1)

One who seeks their own happiness
would pluck out the dart from themselves—
the wailing and praying,
and sadness inside.
The Dart (Snp 3.8 20.1)

With dart plucked out, unattached,
having found peace of mind,
overcoming all sorrow,
one is sorrowless and quenched.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 1.1)

So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying in a forest near Icchānaṅgala. Now at that time several very well-known well-to-do brahmins were residing in Icchānaṅgala. They included the brahmins Caṅkī, Tārukkha, Pokkharasāti, Jānussoṇi, Todeyya, and others. Then as the students Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja were going for a walk they began to discuss the question: “How do you become a brahmin?”
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 2.1)

Bhāradvāja said this: “When you’re well born on both your mother’s and father’s side, stemming from a clean vessel, with irrefutable and impeccable genealogy back to the seventh paternal generation— then you’re a brahmin.”
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 3.1)
Vāseṭṭha said this: “When you’re ethical and accomplished in doing your duties— then you’re a brahmin.” But neither was able to persuade the other.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 4.1)

So Vāseṭṭha said to Bhāradvāja, “Worthy Bhāradvāja, the ascetic Gotama—a Sakyan, gone forth from a Sakyan family—is staying in a forest near Icchānaṅgala. He has this good reputation: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’ Come, let’s go to see him and ask him about this matter. As he answers, so we’ll remember it.” “Yes, worthy sir,” replied Bhāradvāja.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 5.1)
So they went to the Buddha and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, they sat down to one side, and Vāseṭṭha addressed the Buddha in verse:
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 6.1)

“We’re both authorized masters
of the three Vedas.
I’m a student of Pokkharasāti,
and he of Tārukkha.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 7.1)

We’re fully qualified
in all the Vedic experts teach.
As philologists and grammarians,
we match our tutors in recitation.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 8.1)

We have a dispute
regarding genealogy.
For Bhāradvāja says that
one is a brahmin due to birth,
but I declare it’s because of one’s deeds.
Oh Clear-eyed One, know this as our debate.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 9.1)

Since neither of us was able
to convince the other,
we’ve come to ask you, sir,
renowned as the awakened one.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 10.1)

As people honor with cupped palms
the moon on the cusp of waxing,
bowing, they revere
Gotama in the world.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 11.1)

We ask this of Gotama,
the Eye arisen in the world:
is one a brahmin due to birth,
or else because of deeds?
We don’t know, please tell us,
so we can recognize a brahmin.”
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 12.1)

“I shall explain to you,” said the Buddha,
“accurately and in sequence,
the taxonomy of living creatures,
for species are indeed diverse.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 13.1)

Know the grass and trees,
though they lack self-awareness.
They’re defined by birth,
for species are indeed diverse.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 14.1)

Next there are bugs that crawl or fly,
and so on, to ants and termites.
They’re defined by birth,
for species are indeed diverse.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 15.1)

Know the quadrupeds, too,
both small and large.
They’re defined by birth,
for species are indeed diverse.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 16.1)

Know, too, the long-backed snakes,
crawling on their bellies.
They’re defined by birth,
for species are indeed diverse.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 17.1)

Next know the fish,
whose habitat is the water.
They’re defined by birth,
for species are indeed diverse.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 18.1)

Next know the birds,
winged chariots in flight.
They’re defined by birth,
for species are indeed diverse.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 19.1)

While the differences between these species
are defined by birth,
the differences between humans
are not defined by birth.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 20.1)

Not by hair nor by head,
not by ear nor by eye,
not by mouth nor by nose,
not by lips nor by eyebrow,
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 21.1)

not by shoulder nor by neck,
not by belly nor by back,
not by buttocks nor by breast,
not by groin nor by genitals,
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 22.1)

not by hands nor by feet,
not by fingers nor by nails,
not by knees nor by thighs,
not by color nor by voice:
none of these are defined by birth
as it is for other species.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 23.1)

In specific human bodies
you can’t find such distinctions.
The distinctions among humans
are spoken of by convention.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 24.1)

Anyone among humans
who lives off keeping cattle:
know them, Vāseṭṭha,
as a farmer, not a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 25.1)

Anyone among humans
who lives off various professions:
know them, Vāseṭṭha,
as a professional, not a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 26.1)

Anyone among humans
who lives off trade:
know them, Vāseṭṭha,
as a trader, not a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 27.1)

Anyone among humans
who lives off serving others:
know them, Vāseṭṭha,
as a servant, not a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 28.1)

Anyone among humans
who lives off stealing:
know them, Vāseṭṭha,
as a bandit, not a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 29.1)

Anyone among humans
who lives off archery:
know them, Vāseṭṭha,
as a warrior, not a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 30.1)

Anyone among humans
who lives off priesthood:
know them, Vāseṭṭha,
as a sacrificer, not a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 31.1)

Anyone among humans
who taxes village and nation,
know them, Vāseṭṭha,
as a ruler, not a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 32.1)

I don’t call someone a brahmin
after the mother’s womb they’re born from.
If they still have attachments,
they’re just someone who says ‘worthy’.
Having nothing, taking nothing:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 33.1)

Having cut off all fetters
they have no anxiety;
they’ve slipped their chains and are detached:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 34.1)

They’ve cut the strap and harness,
the halter and bridle too;
with cross-bar lifted, they’re awakened:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 35.1)

Abuse, killing, caging:
they endure these without anger.
Patience is their powerful army:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 36.1)

Not irritable or pretentious,
dutiful in precepts and observances,
tamed, bearing their final body:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 37.1)

Like water from a lotus leaf,
like a mustard seed off the point of a pin,
sensual pleasures slip off them:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 38.1)

They understand for themselves
the end of suffering in this life;
with burden put down, detached:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 39.1)

Deep in wisdom, intelligent,
expert in the path and what is not the path;
arrived at the highest goal:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 40.1)

Mixing with neither
householders nor the homeless;
a migrant with no bastion, few in wishes:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 41.1)

They’ve laid aside violence
against creatures firm and frail;
not killing or making others kill:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 42.1)

Not fighting among those who fight,
quenched among those who have taken up arms,
not grasping among those who grasp:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 43.1)

They’ve discarded greed and hate,
along with conceit and contempt,
like a mustard seed off the point of a pin:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 44.1)

The words they utter
are polished, informative, and true,
and don’t offend anyone:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 45.1)

They don’t steal anything in the world,
long or short,
tiny or huge, beautiful or ugly:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 46.1)

They have no hope
for this world or the next;
with no need for hope, detached:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 47.1)

They have no clinging,
knowledge has freed them of indecision,
they’ve arrived at the objective, freedom from death:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 48.1)

They’ve escaped clinging
to both good and bad deeds;
sorrowless, stainless, pure:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 49.1)

Pure as the spotless moon,
clear and unclouded,
they’ve ended relish for rebirth:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 50.1)

They’ve got past this grueling swamp
of delusion, transmigration.
Meditating in stillness, free of indecision,
they have crossed over to the far shore.
They’re quenched by not grasping:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 51.1)

They’ve given up sensual pleasures,
and have gone forth from lay life;
they’ve ended rebirth in the sensual realm:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 52.1)

They’ve given up craving,
and have gone forth from lay life;
they’ve ended craving to be reborn:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 53.1)

They’ve thrown off the human yoke,
and slipped out of the heavenly yoke;
unyoked from all yokes:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 54.1)

Giving up desire and discontent,
they’re cooled and free of attachments;
a hero, master of the whole world:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 55.1)

They know the passing away
and rebirth of all beings;
unattached, holy, awakened:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 56.1)

Gods, centaurs, and humans
don’t know their destiny;
the perfected ones with defilements ended:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.

They have nothing before or after,
or even in between.
Having nothing, taking nothing:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 58.1)

Captain of the herd, excellent hero,
great seer and victor;
unstirred, washed, awakened:
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
With Vāseṭṭha (Snp 3.9 59.1)

They who know their past lives,
see heaven and places of loss,
and have attained the ending of rebirth,
that’s who I declare a brahmin.
